query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Inducing an ultra‐nanocrystalline, dynamically amorphized surface layer on the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy by applying a controlled high-energy mechanical surface treatment will enable a self‐lubricating behavior that maintains low friction and reduced wear rates across a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with a typical coarse-grained microstructure and without any pre-existing self-lubricating surface layer.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled high-energy mechanical surface treatment (e.g., pre-straining or surface deformation process) to engineer a near-surface layer that becomes ultra‐nanocrystalline and partially amorphous.
generation.conditions: Sliding tribological tests conducted from room temperature to 800 °C; loads maintained at levels comparable to prior tribology studies; tests performed in an inert or controlled atmosphere to minimize oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline, dynamically amorphized near-surface layer that exhibits lower shear strength and specific high-angle grain boundary characteristics, akin to the inverse Hall-Petch behavior observed in similar high-entropy alloys.
generation.mechanism: The engineered surface layer promotes dissipative deformation and may develop cavitation-induced nanoporosity under sliding, which together reduce the effective shear resistance. This structural transformation mimics self-lubricating behavior, thus lowering friction and wear over a wide temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated CoCrFeNi samples, the treated alloy is expected to show a significantly lower friction coefficient (approaching or below ~0.3) and reduced wear rates (e.g., an order-of-magnitude improvement in wear volume) consistently from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.baseline: Untreated CoCrFeNi alloy that typically experiences increased friction and wear at higher temperatures due to lack of an engineered lubricious surface layer.
generation.boundary: Effectiveness is projected under sliding loads in an inert or controlled atmosphere across the 25 °C to 800 °C temperature range; performance under oxidative environments or under drastically different load conditions remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The long-term stability of the induced ultra‐nanocrystalline layer under repeated sliding cycles and its behavior under slight variations in environment (e.g., minor oxidation) are not fully resolved.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNi alloy samples: one set subjected to the high-energy mechanical surface treatment to induce the ultra‐nanocrystalline/amorphous surface layer, and a control set with no treatment. Conduct sliding tribological tests across the temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C under identical loads in an inert atmosphere. Characterize the near-surface microstructure (via TEM/SEM) before and after testing.
measurements: Wear rate (wear volume normalized by load and sliding distance)
Microstructural analysis of the near-surface region (grain size, amorphous content, presence of nanoporosity)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction (e.g., >20% improvement) in friction coefficient and wear rate across the full temperature range compared to the control samples, or if the expected ultra‐nanocrystalline/amorphous microstructure is not confirmed by post-test analysis, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
